extracted.intended_audience: individual commenters, advocacy organizations, policy analysts, and legal practitioners involved in filing or evaluating administrative (notice-and-comment) submissions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing credible, effective public comments to federal agency dockets, emphasizing authenticity, specificity, and legal/compliance risks in light of large-scale fake-comment campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mass form-letter/template submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass form-letter campaigns are routinely treated as a single comment by agencies — their political weight is dwarfed by their numerical appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on bulk identical or near-identical template letters. Agencies may aggregate or treat these as one input; numerical volume from identical submissions carries far less persuasive weight than distinct, substantive comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate personal engagement with specifics, dated facts, and named experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions that demonstrate personal engagement (specifics, dated facts, named experiences) gain credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete details such as dates, location-specific impacts, transactions or interactions you experienced, and named persons/events where relevant. These elements make a comment harder to dismiss as generic or inauthentic when agencies or courts inspect authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be original, identifiable, and locally specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Real voices stand out far more in datasets dominated by template fraud — original, identifiable, locally specific comments rise above the noise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide identifying/contextual information (e.g., role, locality, industry or community ties) and tailor content to local or personal consequences. Original narratives or locally grounded data increase the likelihood your comment will be noticed and credited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid easily detectable 'search-and-replace' or copy-paste techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Unsophisticated 'search and replace' techniques — the same base comment repeated with key words swapped each time — made the fakes easy to detect and separate from organic feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each submission has substantive, non-mechanical variation. Repeating a single base text with only token substitutions invites automated detection and removal as inauthentic comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity is not a substitute for authenticity or quality
rubrics_metrics.description: After researchers stripped likely fakes, only ~800,000 authentic responses remained — and the vast majority (up to 99% in some samples) supported keeping net neutrality, opposite the headline numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on producing high-quality, authentic comments rather than maximizing raw counts. Agencies and researchers will attempt to filter out fraud, and authentic comments better reflect and influence the administrative record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not engage in astroturfing; consider legal and enforcement risks
rubrics_metrics.description: The post-2017 enforcement actions against three companies for generating fake comments raised the legal cost of astroturfing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that creating fake or fraudulent comments can trigger investigations, settlements, or other legal consequences. Ensure compliance with laws and terms of service; avoid any paid, automated, or deceptive schemes to fabricate public input.
